ranking.summary: ReAct presents a clear prompting paradigm that interleaves language reasoning with environment actions and observations. Results across knowledge-intensive and interactive tasks support its value over action-only approaches and show strong few-shot performance in the reported settings. The contribution is substantial and influential in concept, though the evidence inspected here is limited to the paper’s summary and selected main-text excerpts; detailed tables, statistical uncertainty, and broader robustness are not assessed.

WebArena contributes a self-hostable, dynamic web environment and 812-task benchmark for evaluating end-to-end natural-language web agents across diverse sites and tools. Its deterministic setup and programmatic completion checks make it useful for reproducible agent research; baseline performance and failure analysis illustrate the benchmark's difficulty, though the reported agents and evaluation provide only an initial view of capability.

OSWorld makes a substantial benchmark contribution by providing a controllable real-computer environment and diverse tasks with per-task executable evaluation, enabling assessment beyond browser-only or static-demonstration settings. Careful construction and human/baseline measurements make it useful, while empirical conclusions remain bounded by its Ubuntu-centered task suite and disclosed evaluation uncertainty.

τ-bench contributes a modular benchmark for tool agents in simulated multi-turn user interactions under domain policies, using database-state goals and pass^k to measure repeatability. Experiments across multiple models reveal substantial weaknesses in the tested setting. The evidence is useful, but simplified customer-service domains and simulated users limit real-world generalization.

SWE-bench contributes a substantial, realistic benchmark of issue-resolution tasks drawn from real GitHub repositories, framing code generation as repository-level engineering evaluated against tests. The reported baselines show difficulty for evaluated models, and the authors clearly identify Python-only coverage and test-based evaluation as scope limitations.

SWE-agent makes a substantial, practically relevant contribution by treating the agent-computer interface as a design variable for repository-level software engineering. Its custom search, editing, feedback, and context-management tools are evaluated on SWE-bench and supported by interface ablations, showing notable gains over the tested shell-only and retrieval baselines. The evidence is meaningful but bounded to two leading closed models and the benchmark/setup described; the paper also reports persistent inefficient agent behavior.

Self-RAG trains language models to decide when to retrieve, assess retrieved evidence and generated segments with reflection tokens, and use those signals for controllable decoding. Across six tasks, its reported results and ablations provide substantial evidence of gains over several retrieval and non-retrieval baselines, especially in factuality and citation measures, though evidence is scoped to particular models, datasets, and evaluation choices.

RULER broadens long-context evaluation beyond single-needle retrieval with configurable retrieval, multi-hop tracing, aggregation, and QA tasks. Its evaluations expose substantial performance degradation and failure modes in ten models, making a useful diagnostic benchmark contribution; the evidence remains tied to synthetic/proxy tasks and a limited model sample.

AGENTLESS presents a deliberately simple repository-repair pipeline—hierarchical code localization followed by sampled patch generation, regression-test filtering, and majority voting—and shows that this design can perform competitively on SWE-bench Lite at low reported inference cost. Its useful additional contribution is a manual classification of benchmark problems and a filtered 252-problem variant, though comparative claims remain bounded by the benchmark and by reliance on reported baseline results.

Introduces CodeAct, using executable Python as a unified, multi-turn action format, and releases a 7k-trajectory tuning set with CodeActAgent models. Controlled comparisons across 17 LLMs and downstream evaluations provide meaningful evidence that code actions can improve complex tool use and enable useful local agents, though gains vary by model and the central benchmark is small and manually curated.

InterCode contributes a practical framework and benchmark formulation for interactive code generation, pairing code actions with execution feedback in containerized environments. Its Bash and SQL implementations and model evaluations demonstrate that the testbed is usable and expose meaningful benefits and failure patterns of interaction, though empirical breadth and task coverage remain limited.

RAFT is a practical fine-tuning recipe for in-domain RAG: train with question/document/answer examples that include irrelevant retrieved documents, sometimes omit the oracle document, and produce quoted reasoning answers. The paper reports improvements over several fine-tuning and RAG baselines across biomedical QA, multi-hop QA, and API-document tasks. Its main value is the targeted training setup and broad task demonstrations, while claims are bounded to a same-domain/document setting and the inspected evidence leaves some evaluation details unresolved.

AutoGen presents a flexible infrastructure for building LLM applications as conversations among customizable agents that can combine models, tools, and human participation. Its contribution is a practical, general-purpose framework demonstrated across diverse workflows; evidence is promising but largely illustrative and task-specific rather than a broad validation of general performance.

Gorilla combines APIBench, AST-based API-call evaluation, and retrieval-aware fine-tuning of LLaMA to improve API selection and call generation across several model hubs. Reported results are strong on the evaluated tasks, while also revealing substantial dependence on retrieval quality and a narrower empirical scope than the paper’s broad API ambitions.

AgentBench offers a useful, broad interactive benchmark spanning eight environments and evaluates 25 LLMs, providing a shared testbed and evidence of substantial variation in agent performance. Its breadth and release are valuable, though claims about practical capability depend on heterogeneous tasks and evaluation procedures, several of which use constructed or automated judging. This assessment inspected the introduction, portions of the task protocols, and conclusion/results snippets rather than the complete paper.

AlphaCodium presents a practical, test-driven multi-stage inference workflow for code generation: it builds problem reasoning and candidate tests, then iteratively runs and fixes code against public and generated tests. Reported gains across several models on CodeContests are substantial, though the evaluation is narrow and comparisons with prior systems are not fully controlled.

This survey organizes the emerging LLM-based autonomous-agent literature around construction, applications, and evaluation, and proposes a four-module framework spanning profile, memory, planning, and action. Its value is primarily structured synthesis and agenda-setting rather than new empirical validation; its broad coverage is useful, while taxonomy coverage and the surveyed literature's early-stage evaluation remain relevant constraints.

Reflexion adds a practical, training-free loop in which an LLM agent reflects on failed attempts and stores the resulting guidance in dynamic memory, using binary success feedback. The reported gains on AlfWorld and HotPotQA are promising, but evaluations are modest in scale and the approach does not improve meaningfully on WebShop, limiting the strength and breadth of the evidence.

CAMEL introduces a role-playing and inception-prompt framework for two LLM agents to collaborate with limited human guidance, alongside scalable conversation-generation pipelines and datasets for AI-society and coding scenarios. Its main contribution is a concrete research scaffold and prompt-design analysis, not evidence of robust real-world task completion.

note: Scores remain absolute; equal scores use task ID as a deterministic display tie-break.
